strengths: Extremely thorough empirical evaluation spanning 29 datasets across 8 diverse task families (fine-grained region classification, bounding-box classification, open-vocabulary detection, image-text retrieval at both short and long caption lengths, zero-shot classification, dense/segmentation prediction, and downstream LMM integration), giving strong evidence that the gains are not confined to a narrow benchmark.

Fills a genuine and previously underserved gap by releasing a suite of Chinese fine-grained evaluation benchmarks (LIT-CN, DCI-CN, DOCCI-CN, BoxClass-CN) and a new 12M-image Chinese region-text training corpus (FineRegion-CN), which should be broadly useful to the community.

Reasonably careful ablations: loss-component ablation (TIC, CMR) showing meaningful drops when removed, a controlled bilingual-vs-English-only data ablation isolating the mutual benefit of bilingual training, and a re-trained-baseline comparison (Appendix E) that controls for training data to isolate architectural/objective contributions from data effects.

Consistent and often large improvements over strong, recent, comparably-sized baselines (SigLIP 2, MetaCLIP 2, FG-CLIP, Chinese-CLIP) across nearly all reported tasks and backbone scales, and demonstrated transfer benefit when used as a vision encoder in a full LMM (LLaVA-1.5) and as a scorer for open-vocabulary detection, indicating practical downstream utility beyond retrieval metrics alone.

Good transparency in the appendix: detailed hyperparameter tuning procedure, dataset composition tables, qualitative visualizations (dense feature alignment maps, TIC embedding separability), and example captions/categories, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: Overall technical novelty is somewhat incremental: the framework largely composes existing ingredients (SigLIP2 backbone, FG-CLIP-style hard-negative fine-grained textual/visual losses, dual short/long caption training as in Long-CLIP-style works, CMR loss from prior work). The main new component, the TIC loss, is a fairly straightforward intra-modal hard-negative contrastive objective and its marginal benefit, while nontrivial, is modest relative to the paper's other engineering contributions.

Potential circularity in the BoxClass-CN benchmark construction: region-text pairs are filtered using region-text similarity computed by FG-CLIP (a prior version of the authors' own model family) with a threshold of 0.15, which could bias the resulting benchmark toward pairs that FG-CLIP-family models are already predisposed to score well on, weakening the objectivity of FG-CLIP 2's strong results on this specific benchmark.

The Chinese long-caption benchmarks (DCI-CN, DOCCI-CN) are produced by machine-translating English captions with an LMM and validating with native speakers, but details of the validation protocol (number of annotators, inter-annotator agreement, error rates) are not reported, leaving open questions about benchmark quality and translation artifacts.

No variance/multiple-run reporting or statistical significance testing is provided anywhere in the paper; given that many performance gaps over the strongest baselines (e.g., SigLIP 2, Meta CLIP 2) are sometimes small in specific settings (e.g., ImageNet-1K/v2 classification, some VOC/PC segmentation numbers), it is hard to assess whether improvements are robust.

Loss weights (λ1–λ4) are tuned via a sequential greedy search directly against validation performance on the same task families used for final evaluation, raising some concern about overfitting the training recipe to the reported benchmarks rather than a more principled or held-out selection procedure.

The Impact Statement is essentially a non-statement ("none which we feel must be specifically highlighted") despite the paper training on hundreds of millions of web-scraped image-text pairs (LAION, Wukong, in-house 500M Chinese data) and releasing large new datasets; potential privacy, bias, and content-moderation issues in the released Chinese region-text and web-derived benchmark data are not discussed.

Backbone comparisons are not always strictly matched (e.g., ViT-L/14 vs ViT-L/16, or comparing FG-CLIP 2 ViT-So/16 against MetaCLIP 2 ViT-H/14 with far more parameters), which the paper acknowledges positively as an efficiency argument but which also complicates precise attribution of gains to the proposed method versus backbone/resolution differences.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning 29 datasets and 8 diverse task families (fine-grained understanding, bounding box classification, open-vocabulary detection, image-text retrieval, zero-shot classification, dense prediction, LMM integration, ablations), with consistent gains over strong recent baselines (SigLIP 2, FG-CLIP, MetaCLIP 2) across nearly all settings and multiple backbone scales (Base/Large/So400M).

Fills a genuine and previously underserved gap: unifying fine-grained (region-level) alignment with bilingual (English-Chinese) capability in a single dual-encoder framework, whereas prior work addressed these axes separately.

Contributes a new and useful set of Chinese evaluation resources (LIT-CN, DCI-CN, DOCCI-CN for long-caption retrieval; BoxClass-CN for region-level classification) that address a real scarcity of fine-grained Chinese multimodal benchmarks, with reasonably detailed construction pipelines and category schema provided in the appendix.

The proposed TIC loss and CMR loss with global threshold synchronization are reasonably well-motivated and ablations (Table 7) show meaningful, non-trivial contributions to hard-negative discrimination (FG-OVD Hard, COCO Top-1), lending some support to the specific technical contributions beyond just data/scale.

Demonstrates downstream transfer value: gains carry over to open-vocabulary detection (via fused confidence with LLMDet), dense prediction (Cat-Seg), and as a vision encoder in LLaVA-style LMMs, suggesting practical utility beyond intrinsic alignment metrics.
Plans to release model, code, and benchmark, supporting reproducibility and community adoption.
weaknesses: Most individual components (sigmoid/SigLIP loss, RoIAlign region alignment, hard-negative textual discrimination à la FG-CLIP, rank/margin loss adapted from Zhang et al. 2024b) are incremental adaptations of existing techniques; the main technical novelty is largely confined to the TIC loss and the global-threshold synchronization for CMR, which are relatively modest contributions relative to the paper's scale of claims.

Much of the reported superiority likely stems from substantially larger and more heavily curated/re-captioned training data (1.6B enhanced LAION captions, 500M in-house Chinese pairs, in-house Chinese region data) rather than the proposed architectural/loss innovations; without data-matched baselines or an ablation isolating the effect of data scale/curation vs. objectives, it is hard to attribute gains to the claimed methodological contributions.

The new Chinese benchmarks are constructed via automated LMM-based pipelines (captioning, translation, detection, similarity filtering) with limited independent quality control beyond brief mention of native-speaker validation for translations only; BoxClass-CN's category set (566 classes derived via clustering/merging with a 0.15 similarity threshold from FG-CLIP itself) risks circularity since FG-CLIP-family models are also evaluated on it and FG-CLIP was used to construct the very filtering criterion.

No error bars, multiple seeds, or statistical significance analysis are reported despite fine-grained differences between methods sometimes being small (e.g., ImageNet-1K/v2, some retrieval numbers), making it difficult to assess robustness of the comparisons.

Some baseline comparisons appear incomplete or inconsistent across backbone families (e.g., missing FineCLIP/CLIPSelf entries for larger backbones, inconsistent ViT-L/14 vs ViT-L/16 designations across tables), and it is unclear whether all baselines were re-evaluated under identical protocols or taken from original papers, raising reproducibility concerns for exact numbers.

Fixed loss weights (λ1–λ5) are stated as chosen for 'stable and effective' training without ablation or sensitivity analysis, and hyperparameter choices such as the 0.95 similarity filter and top-10 hard negative selection for TIC are not justified empirically.

The paper does not discuss computational cost/resource footprint (e.g., 160 NPUs + 16 H800 GPUs for training) in terms of accessibility/reproducibility for the broader research community, nor provide wall-clock/carbon cost estimates.

Limitations section is very brief and mostly forward-looking (longer inputs, relational structures) rather than critically engaging with the identified weaknesses above (e.g., data-scale confounds, benchmark circularity, or potential biases introduced by LMM-generated captions).
